patient_counselling: Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) 100 mg twice daily for 5 days — TAKE WITH FOOD (improves absorption ~40%, reduces stomach upset). Complete the full 5-day course even if symptoms improve in 1–2 days — incomplete therapy causes treatment failure and resistance.
Common nitrofurantoin side effects: nausea, headache, brown-yellow urine discoloration (harmless and expected), occasional GI upset. Take with food to minimize.

TMP-SMX DS (160/800 mg) twice daily for 3 days (alternative first-line if nitrofurantoin contraindicated): take with full glass of water; drink plenty of fluids; avoid prolonged sun exposure (photosensitivity).

Drink plenty of water (2–3 L/day) during treatment to flush bacteria; urinate frequently and completely; void before and after intercourse; wipe front-to-back; avoid bubble baths and irritating soaps.
Cranberry products (cranberry capsule with PAC ≥36 mg/day) have modest evidence for prevention of recurrent UTI per Cochrane; cranberry juice is high in sugar — capsules preferred.
D-mannose is NOT recommended — MERIT trial (2024, JAMA) and Cochrane (2022) found no benefit over placebo for UTI prevention.

Phenazopyridine (pyridium) 200 mg three times daily for up to 2 days (OTC) for symptom relief during the first 24–48h while antibiotics take effect — note: this is a urinary analgesic, NOT an antibiotic; turns urine bright orange/red (will stain clothing/contact lenses); avoid in G6PD deficiency, pregnancy, severe renal impairment.
Symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency) typically improve within 24–48 hours of antibiotic; if no improvement after 48 hours or worsening, return to pharmacy or physician.

Important drug interactions for TMP-SMX: increases warfarin INR (bleeding risk), elevates potassium with ACEi/ARB/spironolactone (hyperkalemia), increases methotrexate toxicity, may increase phenytoin/sulfonylurea levels. Review all medications before prescribing.

Red flags requiring physician referral: fever >38°C, flank pain, nausea/vomiting (suggests pyelonephritis), pregnancy (refer for assessment), male, recurrent UTI (≥2 in 6 months or ≥3 in 12 months), recent antibiotic use, recent hospitalization or catheter, immunosuppression, structural urologic abnormalities, hematuria persisting after treatment, no improvement after 48 hours, suspected STI.
therapeutic_flow: 1. Confirm Minor Ailments eligibility: Ontario female resident, age 16–65, with classic uncomplicated cystitis symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort) without complicating factors; verify ID/OHIP, obtain consent.

2. Focused history: symptom duration and severity, hematuria, prior UTI history (recurrent if ≥2/6 months or ≥3/12 months), pregnancy possibility (urine βhCG if uncertain), comorbidities (diabetes, immunosuppression, structural abnormalities), recent antibiotic use, allergies, current medications, sexual history (STI risk).

3. Red flag screen: fever, flank pain, nausea/vomiting, rigors (pyelonephritis); pregnancy or possible pregnancy; male sex; age <16 or >65; recurrent UTI; immunocompromise; recent catheter or hospitalization; structural abnormalities; severe symptoms; suspected STI (vaginal discharge, new partner) — refer.

4. Differential diagnosis: rule out vaginitis (Candida, BV, trichomonas), STI (chlamydia, gonorrhea — urethritis), interstitial cystitis, urethral irritation, atrophic vaginitis (postmenopausal), pyelonephritis, kidney stones.

5. Therapy selection per PHO Bugs & Drugs 2024: nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) 100 mg BID × 5 days first-line if eGFR ≥45; TMP-SMX DS BID × 3 days second-line if local resistance <20% and no allergy/interactions; fosfomycin 3 g single dose alternative; phenazopyridine 200 mg TID × 1–2 days for symptom relief.

6. Counsel on antibiotic timing (with food for nitrofurantoin), full course completion, hydration, voiding hygiene, expected timeline (improvement in 24–48h), recurrent UTI prevention (cranberry PAC, voiding habits), drug interactions (especially TMP-SMX), when to return for red flags.
7. Document the encounter per OCP standards: assessment findings, diagnosis (uncomplicated cystitis), therapy chosen, counselling provided, notify primary care provider.

8. Follow-up: reassess at 48 hours if no improvement (refer for urine culture and alternative therapy); reassess at end of course; if recurrent/relapsing pattern, refer for urological assessment and possible prophylaxis.
